newsitem.title: GERMANY: OPINION-Wider horizons for German equities.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-Wider horizons for German equities.

text.p: By Hans-Dieter Klein, Head of Equity Research Germany at Deutsche Morgen Grenfell Equity Research

This was the title, topic and tenor of our Equity Research Roadshow early this year. The softening of the DM in particular, the tax reform proposed for 1999, the changes to equity market legislation (share buybacks, law to facilitate capital-raising, special pension funds), the positive effects of the plan for EMU to start in 1999 and last but not least the growing value being created by the companies themselves were shown to be the main forces keeping the bull market on track.
An absence of inflation risks and still low interest rates as a consequence had prompted us to forecast substantial upside for the Dax, given the prospect of the structural changes.

The Dax has advanced a good 50 percent since the beginning of the year and meanwhile breached 4400. The market P/E is now roughly 22 based on estimated 1998 earnings. This compares with the long-term average since 1982 of about 15.7.

The relative valuation of the equity market versus the bond market - to which we attach much greater significance than P/E as a performance yardstick - has deteriorated despite the fall in yields, though, owing to the excellent performance of equities in recent weeks. With a quotient of approx. 1 it is slightly higher than the historical average.

Does that signal the end of the super bull run? Despite the record levels of the equity market and the high valuation by historical standards we consider the risks limited. As long as the positive underlying conditions remain unchanged we expect the market trend to be cheerful - though volatile - but no reversal.

To our mind, the main risk factors as things stand today are: problems of launching European Monetary Union on time, the possibility of Germany's tax reform failing to go through, and - depending on events in the USA - a more rapid rise in yields than expected.

The first two factors will probably not command major attention until after the summer recess in September, and then spark a fair amount of debate. Realistically, both Monetary Union and the tax reform - albeit with some changes - ought to be able to go ahead on schedule.
Given the high unemployment, output gap and lack of scope for industry to pass on higher costs in prices, the inflation risks in Germany and Europe should remain minor until 1998.

Based on this scenario we believe that all in all the market should trend slightly northward in the coming weeks up to September/October before possibly giving way to a consolidation phase. In the medium term, that is on a 12-month horizon, we figure the Dax has the potential to reach 4500-4700 based on our earnings expectations for 1999.
1999 in focus: Continued trend of of improved company earnings

We have now gone on record for the first time with our corporate earnings forecasts for 1999 for all the stocks we cover. The following are the overall results, aggregated, for "listed corporate Germany": Dax earnings improve as in prior years by roughly 14 percent (the tax reform is disregarded).

Aggregated corporate sales, excluding acquisitions, rise by approx. 5 percent, which we consider a very conservative estimate especially since we currently expect only less than 10 percent of all the companies to see sales grow more than 10 percent.
Looking back at 1989 through 1996 we note that 40-60 percent of the companies' reported sales are increasing at a rate of over 10 percent (albeit including acquisitions).
We expect cost structures to improve further in 1999, which holds for materials and personnel expense ratios as well as for depreciation.

The underlying data for our prognoses for 1999 are robust GDP growth of just over 3 percent in real terms, the timely start of European Economic and Monetary Union on 1 January 1999 and the implementation of the long-announced tax reform. We maintain our focus on currency-sensitive stocks.
